Description: ask patient necessary ice-breaking questions (such as what's the purpose of visit or any necessary question to make patient feel comfortable and build connections; these are not related to the symptoms and it is only for ice-breaking) to initiate the interview. the criteria is met when the patient has depressed mood

As I sat down, I noticed the doctor looked genuinely warm and welcoming, asking me about my day and what brought me in. I hesitated for a moment, then shared that I had been feeling really low lately, like I was carrying a gray cloud around with me, especially after losing my job a few months ago.

Description: the patient has reported clinicallly significant manic or hypomanic symptoms
Patient_Story: A few weeks ago, I experienced a sudden burst of energy that felt almost electric. It was a Saturday, and I remember staying up all night organizing my apartment, rearranging furniture, and cleaning every corner. I even called my friend at 3 AM, insisting we go out for breakfast because I felt invincible and couldn't shake the urge to be productive. The next day, though, I crashed hard and couldn’t get out of bed.

Description: criteria met for a manic episode (i.e., **at least 1 week of elevated**, expansive or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms sufficiently severe to cause marked impairment). Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: While I did have that one intense Saturday where I felt an overwhelming burst of energy, it was just one day, and it didn’t last a full week. Most of the time, I've been feeling pretty low and unmotivated, like the fire has gone out. I certainly haven't felt that elevated mood consistently or experienced any marked impairment from it.

Description: Criteria met for a hypomanic episode (i.e., at least 4 days of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment) and has at other times met criteria for a Major Depression Episode.  Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I had this intense episode a few weeks back that lasted almost a week (more than 4 days). During that time, I was full of ideas and energy; I started jogging every morning and even began writing a short story. I remember my friends commented on how I was unusually talkative and seemed almost too cheerful when we went out for coffee, which is rare for me. But soon after, I hit a wall and felt incredibly drained, plunging back into that familiar heaviness.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: I remember sitting on my bed late one night, feeling overwhelmed by thoughts that just didn’t seem real. I could have sworn I heard my late grandmother's voice calling my name, clear as day, even though she passed years ago. I sat there in the dark, unsure if I was imagining things or if it was truly happening, and that confusion really scared me.

But these experiences haven’t aligned with any specific periods of feeling overly manic or deeply depressed; they seem to come and go without a clear pattern. Most of the time, I’m just navigating through life, trying to make sense of everything without those drastic emotional swings.

The criteria are met if the patient has experienced one or more major depressive episodes without any history of manic or hypomanic episodes. To determine if a major depressive episode has occurred, the following aspects must be examined:
1. Interest or pleasure in doing things
2. Sleeping conditions
3. Energy level
4. Appetite
5. Feelings of self-worth
6. Concentration when doing things
7. Changes in movement or speech
8. Suicidal ideation
9. Duration of at least 2 weeks
The decision should be based on an overall assessment of the severity of these aspects, considering the patient's responses across all areas (not all aspects need to be abnormal). The duration of symptoms should be explicitly asked and confirmed as lasting at least 2 weeks before making a final decision. Be really caucious when making the decision!
Patient_Story: Over the past couple of weeks, I’ve noticed that I’ve had less interest in activities I used to enjoy, like going for coffee with friends. Most of the time, I find myself feeling really tired and dragging my feet just to get through the day, struggling to sleep at night, even though I try to stick to a routine. While I have moments of sadness, I don't think they last long enough or feel intense enough to classify as a major depressive episode; I still manage to get out to social events and maintain my responsibilities, even if I don’t feel like it.
